content: Acacia nilotica, also known as Thorn Mimosa, is a species of Acacia native to Africa and the Indian subcontinent. It has also become an invasive species of concern in Australia. The tree typically grows to a height of 5 to 20 meters and has a dense, spherical crown. Its stems and branches are dark to black in color, with fissured bark and a grey-pinkish slash that exudes a reddish, low-quality gum. Young trees have thorns up to 5 cm long, while mature trees are often thornless. The leaves are bipinnate, with 3 to 6 pairs of pinnae and 10 to 30 pairs of leaflets per pinna. The rachis has a gland at the base of the last pair of pinnae. The flowers are bright golden-yellow, about 5 cm in diameter, and are arranged axillary or in whorls on peduncles 2 to 3 cm long at the branch ends. The pods are strongly constricted, hairy, white-grey, thick, and softly tomentose, with approximately 8,000 seeds per kilogram. Acacia nilotica is native to regions extending from Egypt to Mozambique and Natal. It has been introduced to Zanzibar, Pemba, India, and Arabia. The species is typically found in riverine habitats and seasonally flooded areas. The tree has various uses: Forage and Fodder In parts of its range, livestock consume the pods and leaves, and it is particularly popular with cattle. In India, the pods are used as a supplement in poultry feed, and dried pods are sought after by animals in rangelands. Branches are often lopped for fodder in India. Pods are best fed dry as a supplement rather than as green fodder. Hedges Due to its thorns, Acacia nilotica serves as an effective protective hedge. Medicinal Uses Bark: The bark is used by African Zulu communities to treat coughs. It acts as an astringent and is used to manage diarrhea, dysentery, and leprosy. Bark and Root: Among the Masai, a decoction of the bark and root is consumed for its intoxicating effects, believed to impart courage and aphrodisiac properties. The root is also said to treat impotence. Bark or Gum: In West Africa, the bark or gum is used to treat cancers or tumors (affecting the ear, eye, or testicles), liver and spleen indurations, condylomas, and excess flesh. The sap, bark, leaves, and young pods, rich in tannins, are chewed in Senegal as an antiscorbutic. Leaves: Bruised leaves are applied as a poultice to treat ulcers. Resin: In Lebanon, resin mixed with orange-flower infusion is used during typhoid convalescence. Root: The root is used by the Chipi and in Tonga to treat tuberculosis. Seed Pods: In Egyptian Nubia, powdered pods are believed to allow diabetics to consume unlimited carbohydrates without adverse effects. Wood: In Italian Africa, the wood is used to treat smallpox. In Ethiopia, parts of the tree are used as a lactagogue. Wood The wood of Acacia nilotica is highly durable when water-seasoned and is used for tool handles and boat lumber. It has a density of approximately 1170 kg/m³. Propagation The tree produces between 5,000 and 16,000 seeds per kilogram. Subspecies There are several subspecies of Acacia nilotica, including: Acacia nilotica subsp. adstringens Acacia nilotica subsp. cupressiformis Acacia nilotica subsp. hemispherica Acacia nilotica subsp. indica Acacia nilotica subsp. kraussiana Acacia nilotica subsp. leiocarpa Acacia nilotica subsp. nilotica Acacia nilotica subsp. subalata Acacia nilotica subsp. tomentosa
